svg.aria-label: Diagram: how Google Cloud Directory Sync provisions one way from Active Directory, why the default action for a user missing from the LDAP query results is deletion, how two sync instances delete each other accounts by default, and why re-running the sync does not restore the lost IAM access
svg.title: Directory synchronisation: an LDAP query that returns less looks exactly like people leaving
svg.text: An LDAP query that returns fewer results is indistinguishable from people leaving.
And the documented default for a user missing from those results is to delete the Cloud Identity account.
One-way by design, so that Active Directory remains the source of truth
GCDS queries LDAP, then uses the Directory API to add, modify, or DELETE users in your account.
Changes flow AD → Google Cloud, never back. Passwords never sync; AD keeps the credentials.
Runs on-premises or on a Compute Engine VM. Best on a separate machine, not the domain controller.
The default action for a user missing from the LDAP results is DELETE
GCDS lists the Cloud Identity users with no match in the Active Directory LDAP query results.
The query filters out disabled accounts, so DISABLED in AD arrives as ABSENT, the same as deleted.
The default behavior of GCDS is to delete these users in Cloud Identity or Google Workspace.
So a filter typo, an OU move or a partial LDAP result is indistinguishable from a wave of leavers.
Two forests, two sync instances, and a default that makes them fight
By default, users provisioned from a DIFFERENT source will wrongly be identified as having been
deleted in Active Directory. Each instance sees the other instance accounts as gone, and removes them.
Fix: move out-of-scope users into one OU and add an Exclusion Rule, or exclude by UPN suffix regex.
And re-running the sync does not give the access back
#48: after 30 days IAM permanently removes the account. #49: a recreated same-name account is a
separate identity and inherits none of its roles. The address matches; the bindings do not follow.
Which is why Simulate sync is the control: it reports what it WOULD do, and changes nothing.
Adopting an authoritative source means the sole system you use to create, manage and DELETE
identities. Delete authority over Google Cloud access now lives in an LDAP query, off-platform.
#48 gave the allow policy an author you cannot see. #49 gave it a referent you cannot name.
#50 hands that referent a delete button, wired to a query nobody puts in code review.
